title: Cyclic Discrete Diffusion: A Novel Multi-Class Segmentation Refinement Technique
claim: Each element jumps to the next state in a cyclic chain with fixed probability, gradually driving a clean structured output to uniform noise.
layout: 2 stacked tiers, left-to-right; state-cycle graph above, timestep image and bar strip below
description: The top tier shows a chain of six colored circular nodes (road, sidewalk, building, vegetation, car, other). Each node has a self-loop labeled 1-λ and an arrow labeled λ to the next node. A curved arrow labeled λ returns from the last node to the first, which closes the cycle. A boxed 'Transition kernel' on the right gives the piecewise formula for q(x_{t+1}|x_t) with K=6. A dashed line separates this from the lower tier. The lower tier has the input street photo, then segmentation masks at t=0, 4, 8, 12 and 16. The clean mask turns into speckled purple-and-blue noise. Under each mask, a bar chart of per-class probability for a tracked pixel flattens from one dominant bar to uniform bars. A color legend runs along the bottom. The eye goes first to the colorful noisy mask sequence.
caption: Method illustration of the proposed cyclic discrete diffusion (CDD). Each pixel label evolves under the cyclic transition kernel q(xt+1 |xt): it stays in the current class with probability 1 −λ or jumps to the next class (mod K) with probability λ. Starting from a clean mask (x0), the forward process progressively corrupts the segmentation over time (t = 0, 4, 8, 12, 16), driving per-pixel class probabilities to an approximately uniform mixture (shown by the bars). Our model learns a reverse transition pθ(xt−1 |xt) to recover a refined mask.
abstract: We cast image segmentation refinement as a discrete diffusion process. To solve this task we introduce Cyclic Discrete Diffusion (CDD), a novel forward-reverse formulation with a cyclic label topology that maps a discrete label set to the uniform distribution and back. Instead of injecting Gaussian noise as is done for continuous diffusion, CDD evolves segmentation masks through label jumps: at each step, every pixel either remains in its current class or jumps to the next label with a fixed rate. This jump-or-stay mechanism defines a finite-state Markov process with bounded forward and reverse steps, featuring analytically consistent and tractable reverse dynamics. CDD operates natively in a multi-class label space, enabling joint refinement of all classes in a single pass without requiring class-wise decomposition, as commonly needed in prior binary refinement approaches. The proposed formulation admits a finite and controllable number of refinement steps, for which we analyze the convergence properties through spectral gap analysis. We evaluate CDD across diverse segmentation tasks, including multi-class semantic, instance-level, and binary segmentation refinement. Our method consistently improves both region accuracy and boundary quality across multiple backbones and datasets.
